detection.rule_label: Situation Room statement: on-ice call overturned

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Offside): on-ice goal overturned, no goal CHI at 19:05 of period 3
discrepancy.detail:
Video review determined that Chicago’s Taylor Hall preceded the puck into the offensive zone without possession and control and, therefore, was in an offside position prior to his goal. According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Offside” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”

The clock is reset to show 0:56 (19:04 elapsed time), when the offside infraction occurred.

NOTE: In the final minute of play in the third period and at any point in overtime (regular season and playoffs), Hockey Operations will initiate the review of any scenario that would otherwise be subject to a Coach's Challenge.

market_impact.reason: The number of goals in the game changed between the on-ice announcement and the official ruling, inside the same game. Live game-total, period-total and anytime-scorer markets that reacted to the on-ice call were exposed; the post-game box score already reflects the corrected state, so a settlement made from the final official record is not affected. NHL records are not a sportsbook source of record; this is an exposure flag, not a claim that any market was mis-settled.

detection.rule_label: Situation Room statement: on-ice call overturned

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Goaltender Interference): on-ice goal overturned, no goal at 17:36 of period 2
discrepancy.detail:
At 17:36 of the second period in the Stars/Avalanche game, the Dallas requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether Andreas Martinsen interfered with goaltender Antti Niemi before the puck entered the net.  
  
 The Referee determined that Martinsen interfered with Niemi before the puck crossed the goal line. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Referee, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Toronto Video Room, determines that the goal should have been disallowed due to 'Interference on the Goalkeeper,' as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4."

Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Colorado Avalanche.  
  
 Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the Dallas Stars retain their time-out.  
  
 ---  
  
Coach's Challenge  
 1. A team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:  
  
 a) "Off-Side" Play Leading to a Goal  
 A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-Side" infraction by the attacking team.  
  
 b) Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"  
  
 (i) A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; or  
  
 (ii) A play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.  
  
 2. A team may only request a Coach's Challenge if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play.  
  
 3. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out.  
  
 4. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Goaltender Interference): on-ice goal overturned, no goal TBL at 05:25 of period 1
discrepancy.detail:
At 5:25 of the first period in the Lightning/Senators game, Ottawa requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether Erik Condra interfered with goaltender Andrew Hammond before the puck entered the net.  
  
 The Referee determined that Condra interfered with Hammond before the puck crossed the goal line. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Referee, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Toronto Video Room, determines that the goal should have been disallowed due to 'Interference on the Goalkeeper,' as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4."

Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Tampa Bay Lightning.  
  
 Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the Ottawa Senators retain their time-out.  
  
 ---  
  
Coach's Challenge  
 1. A team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:  
  
 a) "Off-Side" Play Leading to a Goal  
 A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-Side" infraction by the attacking team.  
  
 b) Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"  
  
 (i) A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; or  
  
 (ii) A play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.  
  
 2. A team may only request a Coach's Challenge if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play.  
  
 3. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out.  
  
 4. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Linesman, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Toronto Video Room, determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an "Off-side" infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed."

Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Tampa Bay Lightning.  
  
 The clock is re-set to show 13:51 (6:09 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred. Penalty time clocks also were re-set accordingly.  
  
 Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the New York Islanders retain their time-out.

According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Referee, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Toronto Video Room, determines that the goal should have been disallowed due to 'Interference on the Goalkeeper,' as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4 ."

Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Pittsburgh Penguins.Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the Detroit Red Wings retain their time-out.---Coach's Challenge  
 1. A team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:a) "Off-Side" Play Leading to a Goal  
 A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-Side" infraction by the attacking team.b) Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"(i) A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; or(ii) A play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.2. A team may only request a Coach's Challenge if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play.3. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out.4. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

discrepancy.detail:
At 14:18 of the second period in the Red Wings/Panthers game, Detroit requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether Nick Bjugstad interfered with Detroit goaltender Jared Coreau before the puck crossed the goal line.The Referee determined that Bjugstad prevented Coreau from doing his job in his crease, in accordance with Rule 78.7 which states in part: "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Referee ... determines that the goal should have been disallowed due to 'Interference on the Goalkeeper,' as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4."

Rule 69.3 states that goals should be disallowed if "If an attacking player establishes a significant position within the goal crease, so as to obstruct the goalkeeper's vision and impair his ability to defend his goal, and a goal is scored, the goal will be disallowed."Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Florida Panthers.Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the Detroit Red Wings retain their time-out.---Coach's Challenge  
 1. A team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:a) "Off-Side" Play Leading to a Goal  
 A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-Side" infraction by the attacking team.b) Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"(i) A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; or(ii) A play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.2. A team may only request a Coach's Challenge if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play.3. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out.4. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

 A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-Side" infraction by the attacking team.b) Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"(i) A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; or(ii) A play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.2. A team may only request a Coach's Challenge if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play.3. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out.4. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

discrepancy.detail:

Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Colorado Avalanche.Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the Minnesota Wild retain their time-out.

discrepancy.detail:
At 17:31 of the second period in the Capitals/Bruins game, Boston requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether a Washington player interfered with Boston goaltender Anton Khudobin prior to Kevin Shattenkirk's goal.After reviewing all available replays and consulting with NHL Hockey Operations staff, the Referee determined that Washington's Justin Williams interfered with Khudobin before the puck crossed the goal line. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Referee, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Toronto Video Room, determines that the goal should have been disallowed due to 'Interference on the Goalkeeper,' as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4."

Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Washington Capitals.Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the Boston Bruins retain their time-out.---Coach's Challenge  
 1. A team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:a) "Off-Side" Play Leading to a Goal  
 A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-Side" infraction by the attacking team.b) Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"(i) A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; or(ii) A play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.2. A team may only request a Coach's Challenge if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play.3. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out.4. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

discrepancy.detail:
At 12:55 of the first period in the Wild/Red Wings game, Detroit requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether a Minnesota player interfered with Detroit goaltender Jimmy Howard prior to Ryan Suter's goal.After reviewing all available replays and consulting with NHL Hockey Operations staff, the Referee determined that Minnesota's Mikael Granlund interfered with Howard before the puck crossed the goal line. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Referee, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Toronto Video Room, determines that the goal should have been disallowed due to 'Interference on the Goalkeeper,' as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4."Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Minnesota Wild.Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the Detroit Red Wings retain their time-out.

Rule 78.7: Coach's Challenge  
 A team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a GoalA play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.New for 2017-18: If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; orA play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.Updated for 2017-18: A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

discrepancy.detail:
At 6:42 of the third period in the Lightning/Panthers game, Florida requested a Coach's Challenge to review the "Interference on the Goalkeeper" decision that resulted in a "no goal" call.After reviewing all available replays and consulting with NHL Hockey Operations staff, the Referee determined that Florida's Connor Brickley did not interfere with Tampa Bay goaltender Andrei Vasilevskiy before the puck crossed the goal line.Therefore the original call is overturned - good goal Florida Panthers.Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the Panthers retain their time-out.

Rule 78.7: Coach's ChallengeA team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a GoalA play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.New for 2017-18: If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; orA play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.Updated for 2017-18: A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Goaltender Interference): on-ice goal overturned, no goal COL at 17:26 of period 3
discrepancy.detail:
At 17:26 of the third period in the Blues/Avalanche game, St. Louis requested a Coach's Challenge to determine whether Colorado was off-side prior to their goal.After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, NHL Hockey Operations staff determined that Colorado's Sven Andrighetto was off-side prior to the goal. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Toronto Video Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an "Off-side" infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed."

Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Colorado Avalanche.The clock is re-set to show 2:40 (17:20 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.---Rule 78.7: Coach's ChallengeA team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a GoalA play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.New for 2017-18: If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; orA play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.Updated for 2017-18: A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Goaltender Interference): on-ice goal overturned, no goal PHI at 19:01 of period 2
discrepancy.detail:
At 19:01 of the second period in the Bruins/Flyers game, Boston requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether Wayne Simmonds interfered with Tuukka Rask prior to Claude Giroux's goal.After reviewing all available replays and consulting with NHL Hockey Operations staff, the Referee determined that Simmonds interfered with Rask before the puck crossed the goal line. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Referee, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Toronto Video Room, determines that the goal should have been disallowed due to 'Interference on the Goalkeeper,' as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4."

Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Philadelphia Flyers.Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the Boston Bruins retain their time-out.---Rule 78.7: Coach's Challenge  
 A team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a Goal  
 A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.New for 2017-18: If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"  
 A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; orA play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.Updated for 2017-18: A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Goaltender Interference): on-ice goal overturned, no goal COL at 15:56 of period 1
discrepancy.detail:
At 15:56 of the first period in the Avalanche/Penguins game, Pittsburgh requested a Coach's Challenge to determine whether Colorado was off-side prior to Nathan MacKinnon's goal.After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, NHL Hockey Operations staff determined that Colorado's Erik Johnson was off-side prior to the goal. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Toronto Video Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an "Off-side" infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed."Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Colorado Avalanche.The clock is re-set to show 4:08 (15:52 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

Rule 78.7: Coach's ChallengeA team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a GoalA play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.New for 2017-18: If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; orA play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.Updated for 2017-18: A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Goaltender Interference): on-ice goal overturned, no goal CAR at 17:44 of period 2
discrepancy.detail:
At 17:44 of the second period in the Penguins/Hurricanes game, Pittsburgh requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether Derek Ryan interfered with Tristan Jarry prior to Jaccob Slavin's goal.After reviewing all available replays and consulting with NHL Hockey Operations staff, the Referee determined that Ryan prevented Jarry from doing his job in his crease, in accordance with Rule 78.7 which states in part: "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Referee ... determines that the goal should have been disallowed due to 'Interference on the Goalkeeper,' as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4."Rule 69.1 states that goals should be disallowed if "an attacking player, either by his positioning or by contact, impairs the goalkeeper's ability to move freely within his crease or defend his goal."Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Carolina Hurricanes.Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the Pittsburgh Penguins retain their time-out.

Rule 78.7: Coach's ChallengeA team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a GoalA play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.New for 2017-18: If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; orA play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.Updated for 2017-18: A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

discrepancy.detail:
At 2:04 of the third period in the Hurricanes/Lightning game, Carolina requested a Coach's Challenge to determine whether Tampa Bay's Chris Kunitz was off-side prior to his goal.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, NHL Hockey Operations staff determined thatKunitz was off-side prior to the goal. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Toronto Video Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an "Off-side" infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed."Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Tampa Bay Lightning.The clock is re-set to show 18:11 (1:49 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.---Rule 78.7: Coach's ChallengeA team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a GoalA play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.New for 2017-18:If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; orA play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.Updated for 2017-18: A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

discrepancy.detail:
At 11:00 of the third period in the Bruins/Canadiens, Montreal requested a Coach's Challenge to determine whether Boston was off-side prior to their goal.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, NHL Hockey Operations staff determined that Boston's Patrice Bergeron was off-side prior to the goal. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Toronto Video Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an "Off-side" infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed."Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Boston Bruins.The clock is re-set to show 9:14 (10:46 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.---Rule 78.7: Coach's ChallengeA team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a GoalA play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.New for 2017-18:If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; orA play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.Updated for 2017-18: A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Goaltender Interference): on-ice goal overturned, no goal DAL at 10:40 of period 2
discrepancy.detail:
At 10:40 of the second period in the Stars/Coyotes game, Arizona requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether Dallas was off-side prior to the goal.After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, NHL Hockey Operations staff determined that Dallas' Jamie Benn was off-side prior to the goal. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Toronto Video Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an "Off-side" infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed."Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Dallas Stars.The clock is re-set to show 9:30 (10:30 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

Rule 78.7: Coach's ChallengeA team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a GoalA play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.New for 2017-18: If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; orA play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.Updated for 2017-18: A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Goaltender Interference): on-ice goal overturned, no goal ARI at 01:14 of period 3
discrepancy.detail:
At 1:14 of the third period in the Coyotes/Kings game, Los Angeles requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether Arizona was off-side prior to their goal.After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, NHL Hockey Operations staff determined that Arizona's Max Domi was off-side prior to the goal. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Toronto Video Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an "Off-side" infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed."Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Arizona Coyotes.The clock is re-set to show 19:03 (0:57 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

Rule 78.7: Coach's ChallengeA team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a GoalA play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.New for 2017-18: If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; orA play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.Updated for 2017-18: A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Goaltender Interference): on-ice goal overturned, no goal NSH at 03:40 of period 1
discrepancy.detail:
At 3:40 of the first period in the Predators/Coyotes game, Arizona requested a Coach's Challenge to determine whether Nashville's Kyle Turris was off-side prior to his goal.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, NHL Hockey Operations staff determined that Turris was off-side prior to the goal. According to Rule 78.7, "The standard for overturning the call in the event of a 'GOAL' call on the ice is that the Toronto Video Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the Linesman, determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an "Off-side" infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed."Therefore the original call is overturned - no goal Nashville Predators.The clock is re-set to show 16:24 (3:36 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.---Rule 78.7: Coach's Challenge  
 A team may only request a Coach's Challenge to review the following scenarios:1. "Off-Side" Play Leading to a Goal  
 A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the play should have been stopped by reason of an "Off-side" infraction by the attacking team.New for 2017-18: If the result of the challenge is that the play was "On-side", the goal shall count and the team that issued the challenge shall be assessed a minor penalty for delaying the game.2. Scoring Plays Involving Potential "Interference on the Goalkeeper"  
 A play that results in a "GOAL" call on the ice where the defending team asserts that the goal should have been disallowed due to "Interference on the Goalkeeper," as described in Rules 69.1, 69.3 and 69.4; orA play that results in a "NO GOAL" call on the ice despite the puck having entered the net, where the on-ice Officials have determined that the attacking team was guilty of "Interference on the Goalkeeper" but where the attacking team asserts: (i) there was no actual contact of any kind initiated by an attacking Player with the goalkeeper; or (ii) the attacking Player was pushed, shoved, or fouled by a defending Player causing the attacking Player to come into contact with the goalkeeper; or (iii) the attacking Player's positioning within the goal crease did not impair the goalkeeper's ability to defend his goal and, in fact, had no discernible impact on the play.Updated for 2017-18:A team may only request a Coach's Challenge for Interference on the Goalkeeper if they have their time-out available and the Coach's Challenge must be effectively initiated prior to the resumption of play. If the Coach's Challenge does not result in the original call on the ice being overturned, the team exercising such challenge will forfeit its time-out. If the Coach's Challenge does result in the call on the ice being overturned, the team successfully exercising such challenge will retain its time-out.

At 7:06 of the third period in the Golden Knights/Kings game, Los Angeles requested a Coach's Challenge to review whether Vegas' Ryan Reeves caused Los Angeles' Paul LaDue to contact goaltender Jonathan Quick prior to the puck crossing the goal line.

After reviewing all available replays and consulting with the Referee, the Situation Room determined the actions of Reaves caused LaDue to contact Quick, preventing him from playing his position in the crease. The decision was made in according to Rule 69.1 which states, in part, that "If a defending player has been pushed, shoved, or fouled by an attacking player so as to cause the defending player to come into contact with his own goalkeeper, such contact shall be deemed contact initiated by the attacking player for purposes of this rule, and if necessary a penalty assessed to the attacking player and if a goal is scored it would be disallowed."  
  
Therefore, the original call is overturned - no goal Vegas Golden Knights.  
  
 Since the Coach's Challenge resulted in the original call being overturned, the Kings retain their time-out.

discrepancy.detail: At 13:52 of the third period in the Blues/Jets game, the Referee initiated a video review to determine if the puck crossed the Winnipeg goal line between the normal positions of the goal posts. The original call on the ice was "no goal". The Situation Room informed the Referees that the puck entered the Winnipeg net between the normal position of the goal posts. The Referee then awarded the goal to St. Louis because of the actions of Dustin Byfuglien caused the Winnipeg net to become displaced as Brayden Schenn was in the act of shooting the puck into the Winnipeg net. The decision was made in relation to Rule 63.6 which states in part, "In order to award a goal in this situation, the goal post must have been displaced by the actions of a defending player, the puck must have been shot (or the player must be in the act of shooting) at the goal prior to the goal post being displaced, and it must be determined that the puck would have entered the net between the normal position of the goal posts." Good goal St. Louis.

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Off-Side): on-ice goal overturned, no goal CAR at 14:59 of period 2
discrepancy.detail:
Video review determined that Carolina’s Jackson Blake preceded the puck into the offensive zone and was in the process of exiting the ice, however, his skate was still touching the ice when Sebastian Aho entered the offensive zone, therefore, the delayed off-side remained in effect. According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”  
  
Additionally, according to Rule 83.3, “If, during a delayed off-side, an attacking player in the attacking zone elects to proceed to his players’ bench (which extends into the attacking zone) to be replaced by a teammate, he shall be considered to have cleared the zone when both skates are off the ice and the Linesman judges him to have left the playing surface.”  
  
The clock is reset to show 5:11 (14:49 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

Therefore, the clock is reset to show 8:14 (11:46 elapsed time) and no goal Tampa Bay.

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Off-Side): on-ice goal overturned, no goal SJS at 08:56 of period 3
discrepancy.detail:
The play on the ice was challenged under Rule 38 – Coach’s Challenge. Rule 38.1 states, “In all Coach’s Challenge situations, the original call on the ice will be overturned if, and only if, a conclusive and irrefutable determination can be made on the basis of video evidence that the original call on the ice was clearly not correct. If a review is not conclusive and/or there is any doubt whatsoever as to whether the call on the ice was correct, the original call on the ice will be confirmed.”

Video review determined that San Jose’s Adam Gaudette preceded the puck into the offensive zone and was in an off-side position prior to San Jose’s goal. According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”

The clock is reset to show 11:09 (8:51 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Goaltender Interference): on-ice goal overturned, no goal CHI at 11:27 of period 1
discrepancy.detail:
The play on the ice was challenged under Rule 38 – Coach’s Challenge. Rule 38.1 states, “In all Coach’s Challenge situations, the original call on the ice will be overturned if, and only if, a conclusive and irrefutable determination can be made on the basis of video evidence that the original call on the ice was clearly not correct. If a review is not conclusive and/or there is any doubt whatsoever as to whether the call on the ice was correct, the original call on the ice will be confirmed.”

Video review determined that Chicago’s Jason Dickinson interfered with Joseph Woll by pushing his pad, which caused the puck to enter the net. The decision was made in accordance of Rule 69.7, which states in part, “In the event that a goalkeeper has been pushed into the net together with the puck by an attacking player after making a stop, the goal will be disallowed.”

Rule 38.1 states, “In all Coach’s Challenge situations, the original call on the ice will be overturned if, and only if, a conclusive and irrefutable determination can be made on the basis of video evidence that the original call on the ice was clearly not correct. If a review is not conclusive and/or there is any doubt whatsoever as to whether the call on the ice was correct, the original call on the ice will be confirmed.”  
  
Video review determined that Nashville’s Steven Stamkos preceded the puck into the offensive zone and was in an off-side position prior to Filip Forsberg’s goal. The clock is reset to show 2:57 (17:03 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

If a review is not conclusive and/or there is any doubt whatsoever as to whether the call on the ice was correct, the original call on the ice will be confirmed.”  
  
Video review determined New Jersey’s Paul Cotter made incidental contact with goaltender Connor Helebuyck in the crease that impaired his ability to play his position prior to Jonas Siegenthaler’s goal. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 69.1, which states in part, “Goals should be disallowed only if: (1) an attacking player, either by his positioning or by contact, impairs the goalkeeper’s ability to move freely within his crease or defend his goal.”

Video review determined that Detroit’s Elmer Soderblom preceded the puck into the offensive zone and was in an off-side position prior to Michael Rasmussen’s goal. The clock is reset to show 11:51 (8:09 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

If a review is not conclusive and/or there is any doubt whatsoever as to whether the call on the ice was correct, the original call on the ice will be confirmed."

After a thorough examination of all available replays, video review determined that Darnell Nurse’s shot from the defending zone subsequently deflected off the glass before going out of play in the neutral zone at 19:48 (0:12 elapsed time) of the second period. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 38.2 (d) which states, in part, that a team may request a Coach’s Challenge “When a minor penalty for delaying the game has been assessed under Rule 63.2 (iii) for shooting or batting the puck out of play from the defending zone. This will only apply to delay of game penalties when the shot/batted puck is determined to have subsequently deflected off a player, stick, glass or boards, etc., and not a judgment call.”

Therefore, the delay of game penalty assessed to Darnell Nurse was rescinded.

Rule 38.1 states, “In all Coach’s Challenge situations, the original call on the ice will be overturned if, and only if, a conclusive and irrefutable determination can be made on the basis of video evidence that the original call on the ice was clearly not correct. If a review is not conclusive and/or there is any doubt whatsoever as to whether the call on the ice was correct, the original call on the ice will be confirmed.”

Video review determined that Edmonton’s Connor McDavid preceded the puck into the offensive zone without possession and control and, therefore, was in an off-side position prior to Matt Savoie’s goal. According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Off-Side): on-ice goal overturned, no goal BOS at 11:43 of period 3
discrepancy.detail:
The play on the ice was challenged under Rule 38 – Coach’s Challenge. Rule 38.1 states, “In all Coach’s Challenge situations, the original call on the ice will be overturned if, and only if, a conclusive and irrefutable determination can be made on the basis of video evidence that the original call on the ice was clearly not correct. If a review is not conclusive and/or there is any doubt whatsoever as to whether the call on the ice was correct, the original call on the ice will be confirmed.”

Video review determined that Boston’s Michael Eyssimont preceded the puck into the offensive zone and was in an off-side position prior to his goal. According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”

The clock is reset to show 8:18 (11:42 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.

Video review determined Jordan Staal did not have possession and control of the puck as he entered the attacking zone prior to his goal. The decision was made in accordance with Rule 83.1, which states in part, “a player actually controlling the puck who shall cross the line ahead of the puck shall not be considered ‘off-side,’ provided he had possession and control of the puck prior to his skates crossing the leading edge of the blue line.”

NOTE: In the final minute of play in the third period and at any point in overtime (regular season and playoffs), Hockey Operations will initiate the review of any scenario that would otherwise be subject to a Coach's Challenge.

discrepancy.summary: Coach's Challenge (Off-Side): on-ice goal overturned, no goal NYR at 07:08 of period 1
discrepancy.detail:
The play on the ice was challenged under Rule 38 – Coach’s Challenge. Rule 38.1 states\, “In all Coach’s Challenge situations, the original call on the ice will be overturned if, and only if, a conclusive and irrefutable determination can be made on the basis of video evidence that the original call on the ice was clearly not correct. If a review is not conclusive and/or there is any doubt whatsoever as to whether the call on the ice was correct, the original call on the ice will be confirmed.”\

Video review determined that Detroit’s Eeli Tolvanen preceded the puck into the offensive zone and was in an off-side position prior to Oliver Bjorkstrand’s goal. According to Rule 38.9, “The standard for overturning the call in the event of a “GOAL” call on the ice is that the NHL Situation Room, after reviewing any and all available replays and consulting with the On-Ice Official(s), determines that one or more Players on the attacking team preceded the puck into the attacking zone prior to the goal being scored and that, as a result, the play should have been stopped for an “Off-Side” infraction; where this standard is met, the goal will be disallowed.”  
The clock is reset to show 12:57 (7:03 elapsed time), when the off-side infraction occurred.
